articleTitle: A expert system for aid in material selection process
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: An expert system for aiding material selection process is proposed which, in conjunction with TOPSIS (Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Situation), provides a very effective and efficient technique for material selection for a component. TOPSIS is a highly advanced optimization technique which requires that the user provides an index of relative importance for different properties by the author, the relative importance rating to be decided by the designers. However, the designers may not arrive at the same conclusion due to their different rating technique even though they use the same technique. In the proposed method, an expert system has been presented, which uses a small tool called Rulemaster and OPSS (developed at IIT Delhi) that facilitates the development of particular consultant paradigms. In identifying the knowledge base to be included in the system, special care was taken so that different designers get uniform results by using the proposed system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A methodology for project control through risk analysis: the case of a pipeline project
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Projects exposed to uncertainties can be effectively controlled with the application of risk analysis during the planning stages. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), can be used to analyze risks associated with such projects. The results from risk analysis along with activity analysis are combined to develop a logical contingency allowance for the project through the application of probability theory. Effective control of the project is possible by limiting the changes within the allowance for each work package and the utilization of contingency through proper appropriation. This methodology has been applied to a pipeline laying project in India. The example application demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology for project control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Hypertext based distributed object management for information location and retrieval
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Present user communities exchange information through media like electronic mail, computer news groups, information servers, and so on. Old methods and technologies are not able to deal with large amounts of information. This paper discusses an efficient solution for managing information with the help of a hypertext/hypermedia approach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Role of strategic planning in engineering management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Today, more than ever before, engineers are faced with uncertain and sometimes chaotic environments in which to function. The traditional roles of an engineer to design, develop, and streamline a manufacturing process for a product are still valued and relevant. However, the need for an engineer to participate in the process of identifying the product to be developed, the schedule and resources required, and the goal of satisfying the customer, has become paramount to achieving the success of the enterprise. When we include these endeavours in the functions of an engineer, management of "engineering" takes on a new dimension. The ramifications of the changing and increased functions of an engineer and consequent impacts on engineering management are explored. The basic principles which should be invoked in order to embrace the new environment for engineering management are outlined. The ultimate finding of this study is that the enterprise strategic plan should be developed in such a way as to allow engineering management to encompass the full spectrum of the responsibilities of engineers. A consequence of this is that the fundamental elements of the strategic process can best be implemented through a project team or group approach. The paper thus concentrates on three areas: evolving environment, strategic plan, and ways to achieve enterprise success.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Strategic directions for construction project management information systems
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Project management software packages are keeping pace with increases in microcomputer power with more efficient database designs, simpler interfaces, and higher-resolution graphics. Infrequent users find that easy-to-use programs match their needs, but professional planning requirements need larger capacities and more powerful features. These programs incorporate the expanded work breakdown coding and expense reporting that government contractors typically require. The interfaces, however, are often difficult to master.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Project management for an international environment
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: This paper is based on project management experience of various international projects. Most of the projects in principle were thermal power projects. The locations of these projects were in India, Ireland, Italy, the Philippines, Spain, Taiwan and the USA. There were several issues involved in all these projects. However, issues referenced in this paper were relatively critical and have been chosen from different (national) projects. For some issues, the methodology utilized for solving these issues is also discussed. General guidance for managing an international project also forms an integral part of this paper. This guidance, of course, is the knowhow obtained from the experience of several projects. This can be applied to any international project with modifications (if required) depending upon the environment of a given nation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Contemporary management of international power plant projects
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Working in the international arena necessitates coping with rapid and constant changes. This paper highlights some important management concepts for successful businesses in the 1990s. Financing and local supply requirements lead to changes of emphasis in sales activities. Supply management and a global network of subsidiaries and partners ensures high process quality and the possibility to better meet customer demands. This is discussed in the context of the three spheres of world-wide economic influence: Europe, Asia and the Americas. Project management, organization and commercial structure as effective tools of successful projects are highlighted. Examples of large power projects and equipment developments in the "borderless world" are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Managing innovation projects in the transnational firm
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: It has been recognized that, in worldwide companies, the opportunities for innovation and the resources needed for it are often in different locations. The innovation processes then become transnational. Starting from a case study on Nissan cross-border product development, this work shows that, for transnational projects to be successful, a company has to undertake organizational actions in a long-term perspective. Company culture and human resource policy should help shape the organization appropriately, especially to orient it towards the sharing of resources, ideas and opportunities and to leverage local resources to the global benefit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Organisation culture & multinational teaming: select observations in the Gulf region
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: If the concerns of multinational teaming are to be beamed on the fabric of organisational culture with any certitude which would lead to identification of certain generic approaches to handling projects in a borderless world, many field reports need to be collected. In the author's experience of working for such organisations, other concerns of project work related to system integration and the integration of organisational structures have been analysed. Concerns of organisational culture and multinational teaming are, to a certain extent, common to organisational cultures with homogeneous personnel. Yet, at the same time, there is not a total congruence to the concerns of the two set ups. In the latter case, issues of organisational induction and maintenance are quite unique, making project work acquire, in such a context, its own strengths and constraints.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radical novelty in the borderless world; towards teacherless and campus-less learning programmes
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: We intend to restrict and focus our attention on the use of networks and interconnections to facilitate learning. There are already networks such as K-12 operational in the United States forming educational communities. The network based learning should aim at something beyond the traditional isolated learning with machines such as a package to learn algebra. While careful design of computational, visual and communication technologies for thorough and thoughtful learning is essential, researchers have shown that hardware and software alone are not sufficient. A fundamental problem confronting users of such networks is how to discover the existence of resources of interest, including files, services and especially people.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Work culture and multi national teaming
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: With the advent of information technology and shortening of the distances between various destinations in the world, the mega projects are generally planned on universal work culture and manned by multinational teaming. This paper throws light on work culture, its ingredients and essentials. The practical cases of mega projects like planning, design and construction of King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah, King Khaled International Airport in Riyadh, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam are reviewed in this work as they represent the theme of this paper.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adopting new technology for modernisation projects in India-select dimensions of pre and post investment perspectives
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Geopolitical changes around the globe and massive economic compulsions within India, stimulated a series of strategic triggers over the last ten years to motivate corporate leaders to modernise their business as a whole and manufacturing in particular. Advanced technology was initially welcome as a "cure-all" with unbounded enthusiasm but the explosion in demand for CNC/FMS or DCS/PLC/CIM did not permeate all sectors of Indian industries at the expected speed. On the basis of a survey of related research publications around the world and a survey of Indian managers who were involved in early modernisation projects, the study reveals an emerging gap between users' expectations before investment and satisfaction level post investment. The study reveals the importance of knowledge congruence between the vendor as a life time stakeholder in the new technology investment. Future research directions which emerge from the users' perspectives are also recorded.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Intelligent user navigation systems for mine planning and design softwares
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Mine planning and design is quite a complex issue and has emerged as a critical area. A number of software packages have come up (e.g. SURPAC of Australia, DATAMINE of USA) to solve and simplify the problem domain. Each of them has been found to have a typical lacunae-user convenience and navigation. Most of these packages have a modular structure and usually follow a menu-based front end. Despite the availability of manuals, many of the areas are found difficult to handle, resulting in misleading output. The paper gives a broad idea to overcome such difficulties with due emphasis on hiearchical knowledge base, user identification and a hypertext based MMI for such planning and design systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The international world of business-role of HRD in engineering and management education
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The paper examines the present trend in global economy and its impact on the growth of the industries. A review of the present status of free trade blocs with special reference to GATT is presented. The role of HRD in the changing scenario is discussed. Effective methods of honing the HRD to achieve the goals of total quality management are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Human resource management-new paradigms
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The human mind is amoebic in nature, responding constantly to external stimuli. For a given stimulus, the response of a human mind, or an individual for clarity, at different times may be different. Since each human mind is a unique entity, the stimulus-response equation is necessarily akin to a non-deterministic finite automaton. We provide reasons for such an inference. Often, understanding the possible responses and potential problems can significantly contribute to better human resource management. Successful human resource management is often the key to successful projects and with a bit of management foresight, success can be ensured.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Standardizing calibration laboratory practices
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The role of the calibration lab is becoming more and more important in view of the 'global business' environment. Scheduled, regular calibration of test and measuring instruments with measurement traceability to the nationally accepted standards is a prerequisite. Certification to ISO 9000-Quality System Standards becoming a must for exports, the calibration activity being the backbone for quality, calibration laboratory practices have become more important. In the present day industrial scenario, setting up of a calibration laboratory by a small scale industry is mostly uneconomical and impractical as the work load does not warrant an in-house calibration lab and full time calibration experts, technicians. In which case the ideal solution is to choose an outside agency which can provide calibration services as per the requirements of the organization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Corporate excellence for international competition
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Business organizations in many countries now realize that they are operating in a global economy and are subject to threats and opportunities inherent in an environment of international competition. Foreign competition has prompted progressive organizations to take actions that are designed to attain excellence in productivity and quality improvement. The paper presents an approach for achieving corporate (company-wide) excellence by building on the precept that practices related to productivity and quality improvement should be institutionalized. Authors suggest that the potential for producing continuous, company-wide improvement is greater when improvement concepts are integrated with salient company practices. A continuous improvement model is proposed that can be integrated with company activities or strategic planning, development planning, budgetary controls, and pricing actions to produce a framework for achieving competitive excellence.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Inter-organizational technology transfer: some key factors
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Describes a study of inter-organization technology transfer (TT) from research to manufacture in India. First, a model to depict the process of TT is developed. An essential feature of the model is the synthesis of technology transfer with an overall non-integrated innovation process. In order to test the model, a factor analysis of the field study data was performed. The analysis yielded a list of empirically prioritized factors. Critical success factors for TT include: techno-managerial capability of the licensee, familiarity with the technology, user involvement, and mutuality.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fault-tree analysis of technological failures
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The technological development process at the company level in a developing country is a complex, longitudinal process and is laden with many a failure. Failures can be either at the adoption, adaptation or innovation stages. This article, based on a field study of 89 manufacturing firms in the Indian capital goods sector, presents technological failures occurring at different stages. Results show that inappropriate selection, lack of focused adoption, and lack of focused adaptation are the primary causes of technological failures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Going global without leaving your office-using new WAN technologies
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The paper gives an overview of emerging computer and communication technologies for wide area networking, which make it possible for a global manager to have voice, data and facsimile as well as video interaction with various parts of world.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Globalization of multi-disciplinary project management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Business organizations are deriving their greatest gains from being able to get their products to market faster than their competitors. As such, there has been a tremendous shift towards the use of IT techniques in the technical infrastructure, the globalization of socio-economic policies, and the future vision of these organizations. There are many factors which affect the full-scale deployment of IT in organizations, as it will not only make significant fundamental changes in the technical infrastructure, but the reliability and quality of the products, customer service and satisfaction also have to be dealt with. This is due to the fact that as industrial society moves from a low-wage economy to a highly educated society, expectations also grow. In this paper, we examine some of these issues by considering a few case studies. We demonstrate that, although IT is a very important step in the establishment of technical infrastructure for the future growth of business organizations, it requires certain guidelines to be formulated for defining measurement tools, quantitative measures, etc. for measuring productivity; and at the same time it must enhance reliability and, more importantly, customer satisfaction.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience in execution of a turnkey power project in a transnational environment
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Execution of a turnkey engineering project invariably requires close co-ordination among many independent entities both within and outside the organization. The greater the number of such entities, the more skillful and effective is the co-ordination required. However, when a project is undertaken in a transnational environment and more than 10 nationalities are involved, if this is coupled with an extremely short time required to complete the project from grass root stage, the execution becomes more exciting and challenging. The authors describe their experience in the late 1970s of executing a turnkey power project in Saudi Arabia, where all such variables were present. This paper describes some of the methods adopted to execute this project in a transnational environment, and how some of the project management problems were overcome.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Managing projects in a borderless world
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: With the globalisation of the Indian economy, Indian managers have been subject to a number of challenges, Such challenges as : (i) management of Indian companies abroad; (ii) management of multinational companies in India; and (iii) management of facilities and services in other countries. While managing a borderless world might have been learnt on-the-job so far, it has become necessary to offer structured training on this aspect in the schools of management in India. This paper seeks to address some of the issues related to management of projects in a borderless world.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Participatory management: a case study in a high tech Brazilian plant
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The implementation of participative management (PM) in a high-tech chemical plant recently installed in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil is analyzed. This industrial company started with an authoritarian management model and later adopted PM along with a total quality program, aiming at changing the hierarchical structure, at developing a cooperative environment and at improving human relations. It could be observed that in traditionally authoritarian cultures, these changes create conflicts. The conflicts emerged from the lack of clear strategies for promoting the necessary cultural changes at all hierarchical levels. One can conclude that the implementation of PM is affected in cases of crises due to a tendency to apply punishment and authoritarian measures. It is also concluded that the workers' participation is restricted to the search for operational cooperation on the shop floor, being excluded from any higher level of participation. Moreover, the lack of an effective change in organizational culture may turn participatory management into a less evident control mechanism than conventional managerial methods, but also into an instrument for improving productivity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Challenges in engineering management of high technology systems in industrial projects-Indian perspective
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Challenges to manage the whole team work in industrial projects having engineering efforts of multidisciplinary teams are enormous. Coupled with this, the rapid innovation in every field of engineering and information technology systems have made great impacts in technology and its management in such environments. The cultural aspects of companies in particular and countries in general do add to the complexity in such management. The paper discusses these aspects taking examples of electrical, control and instrumentation disciplines, where fast developments are going on in technology itself.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimizing diversity for engineering management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The problem of optimizing diversity deals with selecting from a set a predetermined number of elements so that the elements selected exhibit the optimal variety of characteristics. We propose a framework in which the concept of diversity can be measured explicitly. We begin with the development of a series of interrelated zero-one integer program for modeling the minimum diversity problem. An example is given to illustrate the application of the minimum diversity model. Finally, a collection of parallel mathematical formulations are presented for diversity maximization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Expert system for project management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: With the globalisation of business, the implementation of turnkey projects is becoming increasingly complex. Inputs from different and diverse sources, coordination and synchronizing of delivery schedules, and cost-reduction targets call for powerful, effective and intelligent tools. Without such tools, an unexpected situation can put the project manager under stress which can consequently lead to wrong decisions. Therefore, there is a necessity today for online systems that can diagnose the causes of problems, help the project management to arrive at quick and proper decisions as well as identify ways to take corrective actions. The important parameters for online implementation of such a diagnostic system are the accuracy and speed of the diagnosis. The concepts used to realise these parameters have a strong influence on the selection of the most suitable tool for a given application. Current concepts such as establish-refine and hypothesis-test are explained. Furthermore, the representation of the knowledge in data files along with an appropriate illustration are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An expert system shell for MIS concept selling
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: All investment decisions must be based on sound analysis of the possible outcome of the implementation. A simulation model to help quantify the benefits accruing out of an information system implementation as per specific environment of the user is discussed. The expert system presented may be used as a primary tool by the users who are planning to revamp or install MIS in their organisations. The rulebases can be updated by making new design files. At best it can provide reasonable results depending on the validity of the design file it uses. The system helps those planning an investment into MIS to evaluate the effectiveness of their decision in terms of pay back period and person hours saved. Such analysis can help in quantification of the benefits accruing out of an investment into IT.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Managing innovation projects in the global system
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The scheme of global integration currently coming into place reduces tariff barriers while building other forms of restrictions. It is also not an equal one, with different countries integrating themselves at different levels. To improve these terms, the third world countries will have to develop innovation management. For a number of third world countries, this would consist of locating windows of opportunities and concentrating their resources in a narrow domain. It is argued that flexible production systems and process descaling provides such windows of opportunity today.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Quality management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Quality management is an assurance that an organization does not rest on its reputation alone. They are continually seeking better ways and better products. And at price-performance ratios one can easily justify. Generally, when processes are entered and brought under statistical control, yield improves dramatically. As yield improves, so does productivity. This helps to maintain costs on existing products and present new products at competitive prices, without compromising quality. Product introduction cycles are shortened by a new emphasis on inter-departmental cooperation. Innovative and needed products become available in a more timely manner. New products conform to requirements right from the start. The total quality management system makes an organization more efficient, more productive and more responsive. In simple terms to make the best even better.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Environmental and regulatory issues related to thermal power stations in India
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Coal based thermal power stations carry inseparable adverse impacts on the environment. These impacts can be minimised through adoption of suitable mitigatory measures. The paper discusses areas of environmental disturbances in thermal stations, the means of minimising the disturbances, important regulations of the government of India on environmental protection and issues affecting sustainable development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: World class manufacturing (WCM)
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Global competition is forcing rapid change in all areas of industrial business. The purpose of competing is to win. In manufacturing industry, winning means satisfying your customer completely, better than the best in the world, and making money for your company at the same time. World class means changing the way we view and operate all business functions. WCM is about using manufacturing successfully as a competitive weapon in global competition. In WCM you satisfy your customer by providing high quality service and products at the right price, delivered on time. Customer focus is not only a sign but is fundamental to world class manufacturing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Global resourcing-achieving success in metals industry automation projects through partnerships
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: A major shift in emphasis is occurring in the metals industry. There is a dramatic proliferation of cost-effective mini-mills. One of the keys to the success of mini-mills is their reliance on automation partnerships to bridge the technology hurdles. Partnering is the only practical methodology that OEMs and automation suppliers can consider if they desire to participate with these new-style producers. To be successful over the long term, the automation suppliers' internal organizational structure must be extremely flat, with broad product offerings that are focused only on industrial control and automation. They must be able to react globally to customer needs in minimal time and provide accurate proposals first time. They must have partners who address control and information systems in every application in the metals industry and be able to provide the technology to support them. They must be able to drive decision-making to the lowest levels practical in the organization. Finally, they must be committed to product quality, with total commitment to customer satisfaction, no matter where in the world they are doing business.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Organizational preparedness
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Effective technology management depends mostly on the emphasis laid by the organization on learning at all levels. This paper, based on several case studies and empirical analyses of over 200 organizations, describes the organizational issues involved in successful technological transformation. Flexibility planning, emphasis on training and development, and unique experiments such as gang-planks (gatekeepers) facilitate technological innovation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of cost accounting concepts in managing IT projects
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Project costing is about the accounting of costs incurred on a project for the purpose of controlling them and planning the optimum utilization of resources. Cost centers in an organization are identified. All projects executed belong to one of the cost centers. Direct costs of an IT project, such as people and materials, are identified. The costs of an organization's support services and other overheads are pro-rated to the cost centers and from there to the projects within the cost centers, using the direct method of cost allocation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Endogenous social factors and dimensions of technology diffusion in a developing country-an Indian experience
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Technology change involves technical and non-technical parameters. A conducive synergic climate involving all these dimensions is essential for successful technology transfer. This is particularly true in the case of developing societies, as their informational, organizational and social environment is not sophisticated enough for that required for successful technology. The author examines a particular case, that of the Green revolution, as an experiment that has succeeded in terms of the various dimensions mentioned above, assimilating the endogenous factors that are intrinsic to the globalization of the social and technical process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Emerging issues in information technology: an international perspective revisited
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The discipline of management information systems (MIS) has been in existence for about 30 years. During this period, the adoption and diffusion of MIS has been significant in the more advanced nations. The advancements in recent years of information technology have been especially rapid transforming industrialized societies from service to information economies. Today, this field continues to be very dynamic, driven by rapid growth in information technology and rising user expectations. Consequently, the key MIS issues and the areas prime for research keep changing and evolving and the perceptions of information management professionals relative to trends in information technology (IT) continues to be of interest to researchers in the field. Other developed and developing countries are also beginning to assimilate information technology into their developmental infrastructure. In this context, it would be useful to identity the key MIS issues and areas for research for both developed and developing nations in variegated social/economic/political systems. This study examines the perceptions of IT professionals in selected countries. The results of studies conducted in these countries are presented in juxtaposition and discussed in the context of earlier studies. As expected, there are similarities as well as a number of striking differences in the perceived importance of various IT issues from study to study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flexible systems approach to management in a borderless world
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: The managerial issues in a borderless world are becoming far more intricate and complex and requires to be handled differently at different levels in diverse situations. There is a need to resolve the paradoxes in literature regarding various schools of thought, and as a response to this a flexible systems approach to management is presented as a spectral and integrative paradigm. The critical managerial issues in the borderless world are outlined, and the utility of this spectral and integrative paradigm is emphasized for handling them effectively.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Enterprise integration system-a new paradigm for information management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Proposes a futuristic approach to managing information. The 1960s and 1970s have seen a growth in structuring information flows. The 1980s saw the advent of management information systems (MIS). In the 1990s, computer integrated manufacturing (CIM) is picking up, and towards 2000, we are heading for enterprise integration systems (EIS). The ingredients of EIS, i.e. the information integration platforms and the technologies of televirtuality, object-oriented databases, hypertext and high-speed data networking, are discussed, and it is explained how these can be used in a synchronized and integrated manner to achieve EIS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cultural complexity and the improved performance of large international projects
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Two popular models are used to describe the main organizational culture types, with specific reference to functional and project organizations. Some important characteristics of national cultures are then examined, based on published research. Two examples of well known major projects are taken to explore the possible (or known) impact of these two dimensions-organizational and national culture on the success of a project. In conclusion, the paper stresses the importance of achieving a 'total' culture fit, within and between, the contracting organizations. Some ideas on the ways in which this 'fit' might be engineered are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Concurrent engineering and its application in turnkey projects management
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Concurrent engineering (CE), also called simultaneous engineering, results from synthesising two fundamental observations. The first is that changes become more and more costly, the later in a project they are done and the second is that doing the different steps of a project in parallel i.e. simultaneously or concurrently gets the project done faster. CE breaks down departmental barriers it involves a multifunction team and integrates concepts and technique of design for manufacturing (DFM), quality function deployment (QFD), continuous process improvement (CPI) and total quality management (TQM) to achieve high quality output in the shortest time. The paper elucidates the concepts, advantages and implementation of concurrent engineering and further discusses its application in turnkey engineering project management.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A sphenomorphic model for the management of the complex environment of a concurrent engineering programme
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Introduces a new model of the innovation management process as it applies to the complex environment of a concurrent engineering programme. By looking in detail at the process, the question "Can innovation be managed?" is addressed. Current ideas on managing complexity and chaotic systems are used to develop a recursive model which, from its wedge-like shape (with a narrowing area of emphasis from project start to deadline), is termed a "sphenomorph". A hierarchical collection of sphenomorphs from many mini-projects combine to form the complete innovation process. Each sphenomorph comprises four distinct stages (diversity, decimation, development, dedication), each requiring a different management style for success. The need for adaptive managers, capable of dealing with all four stages of the innovation process, is considered, and methods are reviewed whereby such management characteristics may be identified and encouraged through appropriate training and development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Policy strategies for economic development of developing countries telecommunications sector
publicationTitle: Proceedings of Engineering Management Society Conference on Managing Projects in a Borderless World
abstract: Many developing countries have lost their economic and competitive position in the world today. They lack the strong transport infrastructure, power generating capabilities and the telecommunications network necessary for efficiently conducting commerce, international trade and social and economic development. Privatisation and liberalisation of most of the key sectors including the telecommunications sector, must be carefully examined to ensure that privatisation brings full economic and social benefits to everyone. With this change, effective policies must be implemented for all these sectors. The paper examines some of these policy issues and strategies for the telecommunications industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
